metadata.methods_description: Participants sat in a Biodex chair in a quiet, dimly lit room and completed seven tasks per session (mental arithmetic, auditory 2-back, motor imagery, passive motor, active motor, N-back arithmetic, and a combined full task). Each task lasted 3 minutes with 30 s rests, in random order, and auditory stimuli were delivered via MATLAB/Psychtoolbox. EEG was recorded with 32 channels (10-20 system), together with fNIRS (prefrontal and sensorimotor montages), ECG (Delsys Trigno), and Biodex torque. The Karolinska Sleepiness Scale was administered before each session and mental load ratings after each task.

citation_details.title: Analysis plan, registered retrospectively: Does scale buy task invariance? Zero-shot cross-task EEG workload decoding with foundation models
citation_details.author: Abinaya G
citation_details.abstract: RETROSPECTIVE REGISTRATION, NOT A PREREGISTRATION. This registration was made on 7 November 2026, after all analyses in the plan had been run. It deposits, unedited, the analysis plan written before the foundation-model analyses (osf_preregistration.md, last modified 3 November 2026) and the earlier working plan (experiment_plan.md, 30 October 2026), with a note on timing (README_timing.md). No independent timestamp shows that the plan predates the analyses. The study compares frozen EEG foundation models (LaBraM, CBraMod, REVE) with log band power for zero-shot cross-task workload decoding on COG-BCI (MATB-II and N-Back), with an external check on OpenNeuro ds007554. Code, results and their commit history: https://github.com/abinaya-g/cross-task-eeg-cogbci (branch revision-reanalysis, folder fm/).

citation_details.title: Predicting Cognitive Tasks from Single-Channel EEG through Task-Semantic Alignment
citation_details.author: Ryota Kanai
citation_details.abstract: Studies of data scaling in electroencephalography (EEG) and related noninvasive recordings suggest that simple wearable devices could eventually reveal more about cognitive states. However, publicly available EEG data are difficult to combine. Different laboratories record different tasks, participants, and devices. Task-agnostic self-supervised learning can exploit such data, but representations learned only with EEG signals have not consistently produced feature representations that are directly effective for decoding the cognitive state. We therefore aimed to incorporate task information by embedding experimental instructions, stimuli and response demands in a common semantic space, and trained an EEG encoder to align signals from a single anterior--posterior differential channel with those task vectors. This framework supports zero-shot prediction without target-condition calibration and few-shot prediction using labeled samples. On a reserved ten-class evaluation, the highest observed zero-shot balanced accuracy was 30.13% (chance 10%). In a separate developmental few-shot experiment, balanced accuracy reached 34.47% using 16 labeled EEG examples per class from another participant, and 74.99% using examples from the test participant's own task recording. Our experiments suggest that training models on datasets with multiple tasks per participant appeared useful, whereas adding datasets containing only one or a few tasks sometimes reduced established performance despite broader task coverage. These exploratory results suggest that EEG datasets that repeat varied cognitive tasks and everyday activities within the same individuals across days, devices and independent studies would be particularly useful for training an EEG foundation model for predicting cognitive states.

citation_details.title: Towards fNIRS foundation models: A curated corpus of 67 public datasets with channel positions in MNI space
citation_details.author: Santiago Posso-Murillo
citation_details.abstract: Brain foundation models have transformed medical artificial intelligence and computational neuroscience by reducing the reliance on task-specific data through large-scale pretraining. While they have been successful with non-invasive neuroimaging data, their adoption in functional near-infrared spectroscopy (fNIRS) has lagged due to the limited size and heterogeneity of public datasets, which are collected under varying protocols, devices, and sensor configurations. In addition, no single fNIRS dataset is comparable in size to the largest datasets in functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI), electroencephalography (EEG), or magnetoencephalography (MEG). The fNIRS datasets are also spread across different platforms and often have insufficient information, or lack the protocols that would make them easier to use. Given the advances in EEG foundation models that enable flexible modeling across diverse EEG montages, we curated 1,955 hours of fNIRS data from 67 public datasets spanning 2,798 participants, representing the largest fNIRS curation effort to date. The curated data include oxygenated (HbO) and deoxygenated (HbR) hemoglobin signals along with the three-dimensional position of every channel in the standard space of the Montreal Neurological Institute (MNI), which makes positions comparable across datasets. We release dataloaders that handle each dataset automatically, along with the minimal preprocessing pipeline used to prepare the data, at https://github.com/sposso/fnirs-datasets. This work aims to facilitate the future development of foundation models for fNIRS.

citation_details.title: NeuroGate: waveform translation between brain
citation_details.author: Ali Zareh, Mehmet Kemal Özdemir, Rufeyda Yagci
citation_details.abstract: The brain processes information across distributed circuits, yet a typical experiment records only a few regions, leaving the rest unobserved. Connectivity and latent-embedding methods relate brain regions but do not return the waveform of an unrecorded one. Here we introduce NeuroGate, a framework for cross-regional neural signal translation that recovers an unrecorded region's waveform from a recorded one. Across 56 pathways spanning rodent LFP, human sEEG and ECoG, and scalp EEG, NeuroGate predicts waveforms more accurately than 13 deep-learning and linear baselines, with low across-session variance and high median accuracy. We tested the predictions against a circuit perturbation: silencing piriform-cortex output with tetanus toxin light chain collapsed piriform-to-bulb predictions in 8 of 8 folds while the reverse was preserved, matching the monosynaptic anatomy. We demonstrate two applications: quantifying how recording redundancy bounds the information from each added source, and a reusable perturbation protocol for verifying directional translation in any circuit.
